title: Observational units
text:
The original third rule
The original definition from the 2014 Tidy Data paper is:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

An observational unit is the kind of thing you’re observing, for example a song, a patient, or a hospital visit. The third rule says different kinds of things belong in different tables.

title: Observational units
section: Problem 5: one unit in many tables
text:
Problem 5: one unit in many tables
This is the opposite problem, where the same kind of observation is split across many files, for example one file per year or one file per hospital site. If the files have the same columns, we can stack them together with bind_rows(), or give read_csv() all the file names at once.

title: Observational units
text:
How hospitals store data
Hospital databases follow the paper’s third rule. Each kind of observational unit gets its own table, and the tables are linked together by ID columns.

patients has one row per patient
encounters has one row per visit, with the patient’s ID
conditions, medications, and observations have one row per record, with the patient and encounter IDs

To analyze the data, we join the tables we need into one tidy table.
Synthea creates fake, but realistic, patient records that are stored this way. Its downloads page has samples of 100 patients as CSV files, and in the HL7 FHIR and C-CDA formats.

title: Observational units
text:
Beyond CSVs: health data standards
In practice, health data usually doesn’t come to us as a folder of CSV files. It’s stored and shared using data standards.

HL7 is the family of standards hospital systems use to exchange clinical data
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is HL7’s newer standard, where data like a patient, an encounter, or an observation is sent as a “resource” through web APIs
The OMOP Common Data Model, from the OHDSI community, is a shared database layout for observational health data, so the same analysis code can run on databases from many hospitals

All of these follow the same idea as the paper’s third rule, with one table (or resource) for each kind of observational unit, linked together by IDs.

Two kinds of questions
When we want to predict something, the type of outcome tells us what kind of model to use.

section: Linear regression: the line of best fit
text:
Linear regression: the line of best fit
\[
\text{price} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{sqft}
\]

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, where the line crosses the y axis
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, how much the price changes for each extra square foot

The “best” line is the one with the smallest squared vertical distances between the line and the data points.

What is tidy data?


Each variable is a column; each column is a variable
Each observation is a row; each row is an observation

The original Tidy Data paper from 2014 defines it a little differently:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

title: Tidy data

Five ways data gets messy
The Tidy Data paper lists five common ways data gets messy:

Column headers are values, not variable names
Multiple variables are stored in one column
Variables are stored in both rows and columns
Multiple types of observational units are stored in the same table
A single observational unit is stored in multiple tables

section: Linear regression: the line of best fit
text:
Linear regression: the line of best fit
\[
\text{price} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{sqft}
\]

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, where the line crosses the y axis
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, how much the price changes for each extra square foot

The “best” line is the one with the smallest squared vertical distances between the line and the data points.

text:
What is tidy data?


Each variable is a column; each column is a variable
Each observation is a row; each row is an observation
Each value is a cell; each cell is a single value



Rules from R for Data Science (2e), chapter 5. Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst, from the Openscapes blog (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
The original definition (2014)
The original Tidy Data paper from 2014 defines it a little differently:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

The third rule is really about databases, where data is split into separate tables and joined back together. The newer definition replaces it with “each value is a cell”. We’ll come back to observational units in Lecture 2, in the Observational units section.

title: Tidy data
text:
Why bother?

Once our data is tidy, we can use the same tools every time we summarize, plot, or model it.


Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
Five ways data gets messy
The Tidy Data paper lists five common ways data gets messy:

Column headers are values, not variable names
Multiple variables are stored in one column
Variables are stored in both rows and columns
Multiple types of observational units are stored in the same table
A single observational unit is stored in multiple tables

We’ll go through the first three using the datasets from the paper. Problems 4 and 5 are about observational units, which we’ll cover in Lecture 2’s Observational units section.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Visualization: ask a question, then answer it
text:
Visualization: ask a question, then answer it

When we make a plot, we’re trying to answer a question about our data. A good plot answers that question clearly.


Artwork by Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
ggplot2: three parts
Every ggplot2 plot is built from the same parts:

Aesthetic mappings, which map columns to visual properties (x, y, colour, fill)
Geometric objects (geoms), which say how to draw them (geom_point(), geom_histogram(), geom_bar())
Scales and labels for the axes, colours, and titles

We add each layer, one at a time, with +.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Scatter plot: two quantitative variables
Is a penguin’s body mass related to its flipper length?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Add colour and labels

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  )

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Histogram: one quantitative variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 250, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable
text:
Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Island", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Rules of thumb

Answer one question per plot
Label axes, with units
Use colourblind-friendly palettes
Avoid pie charts, 3D, and tables of numbers when a plot will do

section: Visualization: ask a question, then answer it
text:
Visualization: ask a question, then answer it

When we make a plot, we’re trying to answer a question about our data. A good plot answers that question clearly.


Artwork by Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
ggplot2: three parts
Every ggplot2 plot is built from the same parts:

Aesthetic mappings, which map columns to visual properties (x, y, colour, fill)
Geometric objects (geoms), which say how to draw them (geom_point(), geom_histogram(), geom_bar())
Scales and labels for the axes, colours, and titles

We add each layer, one at a time, with +.

  geom_histogram(binwidth = 250, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +

Answer one question per plot

title: Observational units
text:
The original third rule
The original definition from the 2014 Tidy Data paper is:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

An observational unit is the kind of thing you’re observing, for example a song, a patient, or a hospital visit. The third rule says different kinds of things belong in different tables.

section: Problem 5: one unit in many tables
text:
Problem 5: one unit in many tables
This is the opposite problem, where the same kind of observation is split across many files, for example one file per year or one file per hospital site. If the files have the same columns, we can stack them together with bind_rows(), or give read_csv() all the file names at once.

title: Observational units
text:
How hospitals store data
Hospital databases follow the paper’s third rule. Each kind of observational unit gets its own table, and the tables are linked together by ID columns.

patients has one row per patient
encounters has one row per visit, with the patient’s ID
conditions, medications, and observations have one row per record, with the patient and encounter IDs

To analyze the data, we join the tables we need into one tidy table.
Synthea creates fake, but realistic, patient records that are stored this way. Its downloads page has samples of 100 patients as CSV files, and in the HL7 FHIR and C-CDA formats.

title: Observational units
text:
Beyond CSVs: health data standards
In practice, health data usually doesn’t come to us as a folder of CSV files. It’s stored and shared using data standards.

HL7 is the family of standards hospital systems use to exchange clinical data
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is HL7’s newer standard, where data like a patient, an encounter, or an observation is sent as a “resource” through web APIs
The OMOP Common Data Model, from the OHDSI community, is a shared database layout for observational health data, so the same analysis code can run on databases from many hospitals

All of these follow the same idea as the paper’s third rule, with one table (or resource) for each kind of observational unit, linked together by IDs.

text:
Question: among men who received blood transfusions during radical prostatectomy, is the storage age of the transfused red blood cells associated with prostate cancer recurrence? (Cata et al., 2011)
Recurrence is a yes/no outcome, so we use logistic regression and report odds ratios. This section follows the analysis and tidymodels chapters of Data Science for the Biomedical Sciences.
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)
We’ll start from blood, which you made in the Coded variables exercise. The code below makes it again, so this page works on its own. The outcome must be a factor, and its second level (yes) is the event the model predicts.
blood <- blood_storage |>
  mutate(
    recurrence = factor(Recurrence, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("no", "yes")),
    rbc_age_group = factor(RBC.Age.Group, levels = 1:3,
                           labels = c("younger", "middle", "older"))
  )

title: Logistic regression
text:
Exercise 1: Fit a logistic regression
Logistic regression models the log-odds of the event:
\[
\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \dots
\]
where \(p\) is the probability of recurrence. Exponentiating a coefficient, \(e^{\beta}\), gives an odds ratio.

  geom_bar(position = "fill")

These exercises go further than the Logistic regression section of the lab. Once you’ve tried them, check your answers against the solutions.
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)
They start from the lab’s blood data, and the last exercise uses cmv, from Extra practice: cleaning and tidying. The code below makes both again, so this page works on its own.
blood <- blood_storage |>
  mutate(
    recurrence = factor(Recurrence, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("no", "yes")),
    rbc_age_group = factor(RBC.Age.Group, levels = 1:3,
                           labels = c("younger", "middle", "older"))
  )

cmv <- cytomegalovirus |>
  mutate(
    cmv = factor(cmv, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("no", "yes")),
    recipient.cmv = factor(recipient.cmv, levels = c(0, 1),
                           labels = c("negative", "positive")),
    donor.cmv = factor(donor.cmv, levels = c(0, 1),
                       labels = c("negative", "positive"))
  )

title: Extra functions for the homework
Extra functions for the homework
text:
mdy(): dates from text
lubridate, which loads with the tidyverse, turns text into real dates. We pick the function named after the order of the date’s parts: mdy() for month/day/year, dmy() for day/month/year, and ymd() for year-month-day.

mdy("1/5/2015")

[1] "2015-01-05"

dmy("5/1/2015")

[1] "2015-01-05"

ymd("2015-01-05")

[1] "2015-01-05"


All three are the 5th of January, 2015.

title: Extra functions for the homework
section: geom_col(): bars from numbers we already have
text:
geom_col(): bars from numbers we already have
geom_bar() counts the rows for us. When our table already has the numbers, geom_col() draws them as they are. These two plots are the same.
# geom_bar() counts the rows for each species
ggplot(penguins, aes(y = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Number of penguins", y = "Species")
# geom_col() draws the counts that count() already made
penguins |>
  count(species) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = species)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Number of penguins", y = "Species")

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)
opt_clean, made at the top of the Linear regression page:
opt_clean <- opt |>
  mutate(
    Birth.outcome = str_trim(Birth.outcome),
    Group = factor(Group, levels = c("C", "T"),
                   labels = c("control", "treatment"))
  ) |>
  filter(Birth.outcome == "Live birth") |>
  select(PID, Clinic, Group, Age, BMI, Birthweight, GA.at.outcome)

title: Solutions: Linear regression
text:
Exercise 1: Fit a linear regression

ggplot(opt_clean, aes(x = Group, y = Birthweight)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Group", y = "Birth weight (g)")








(1) The two groups look almost the same, with a long tail of very light babies in both.

bw_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(Birthweight ~ Group, data = opt_clean)

bw_tidy <- tidy(bw_fit, conf.int = TRUE)
bw_tidy

# A tibble: 2 × 7
  term           estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>             <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)      3259.       29.3   111.      0        3201.    3317. 
2 Grouptreatment    -21.0      41.2    -0.510   0.610    -102.      59.9



The intercept, 3259 g, is the control group’s mean birth weight.
The treatment coefficient, -21 g, is the difference between the treatment and control means.
Its 95% confidence interval, -102 to 60 g, includes 0 (p = 0.61): no evidence that the treatment changed birth weight.

The group means show where the intercept and the treatment coefficient come from:

opt_clean |>
  group_by(Group) |>
  summarize(n = n(), mean_birthweight = mean(Birthweight))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  Group         n mean_birthweight
  <fct>     <int>            <dbl>
1 control     391            3259.
2 treatment   402            3238.

Exercise 1: Adjust for other risk factors

  fit(recurrence ~ rbc_age_group + Age + PVol + PreopPSA + factor(TVol),
      data = blood)

4 Age                  1.03      0.0245    1.09    0.275    0.980        1.08  
5 PVol                 1.00      0.00653   0.00702 0.994    0.987        1.01  
6 PreopPSA             1.06      0.0245    2.44    0.0148   1.01         1.12

8 factor(TVol)3       22.8       1.07      2.93    0.00339  4.26       429.

  summarize(across(c(Age, PVol, PreopPSA, TVol), \(x) sum(is.na(x))))

1   0    9        3    6



glm() drops rows with missing PVol, PreopPSA or TVol.
Storage age still shows no association.
Each 1 ng/mL of preoperative PSA multiplies the odds of recurrence by 1.06 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.12).
Larger tumour volumes (TVol 2 and 3, compared with 1) have much higher odds of recurrence, but very wide confidence intervals: few men in the lowest tumour-volume group had a recurrence.

section: Exercise 4: What does this model ignore?
text:
Exercise 4: What does this model ignore?
Time. The men were followed for different lengths of time (TimeToRecurrence), and some left the study before a recurrence could be seen (Censor). Logistic regression only asks whether recurrence happened; survival analysis, as the original study used, also models when.

title: Solutions: Extra practice: logistic regression
text:
Exercise 5: Cytomegalovirus

cmv_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(cmv ~ donor.cmv + recipient.cmv + time.to.transplant, data = cmv)

cmv_or <- tidy(cmv_fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
cmv_or

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  term                  estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)              0.153   0.697     -2.70   0.00702   0.0329     0.534
2 donor.cmvpositive        1.86    0.613      1.01   0.311     0.558      6.37 
3 recipient.cmvpositive    5.42    0.657      2.57   0.0101    1.60      22.1  
4 time.to.transplant       1.00    0.00738    0.0253 0.980     0.985      1.01 


A CMV-positive recipient has 5.4 times the odds of reactivation (95% CI 1.6 to 22.1). With only 64 patients, every interval is wide.
